summary: Wilhelm Koppers worked in Indology, religious studies, and history/archaeology. He studied under Wilhelm Schmidt at Missionshaus St. Gabriel and earned his Ph.D. at the University of Vienna, where he served as Privatdozent (1924–1938) and Professor and Director (1945–1957).

Wilhelm Krause specialized in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He earned a Ph.D. from the University of Vienna (1936) and completed his habilitation at the University of Graz, where he served as Lektor (1960) and eo. Professor (1968).

Wilhelm Max Müller was a scholar of history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1883–1885) and the University of Leipzig (~1885–1888), and later held a post at the University of Pennsylvania (~1910–1919).

Wilhelm Pertsch was a scholar of Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied under Franz Bopp and Albrecht Weber in Berlin, and under Rudolf von Roth in Tübingen, later serving as Direktor at Schloss Friedenstein from 1874.

Wilhelm Printz worked in Indology and linguistics. He earned his Ph.D. in Berlin under Heinrich Lüders and completed his habilitation at Goethe University Frankfurt, later serving as librarian for the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft and extraordinary professor at the University of Halle (1929–1939).

Wilhelm Rau worked in Indology and linguistics, studying at Leipzig, Marburg (Ph.D. under Johannes Nobel), and under Shanti Bhikshu Shastri. He served as Professor at Goethe University Frankfurt (1955) and Ordinarius at the University of Marburg (1957–1988).

Wilhelm Scherer worked in linguistics and related fields. He earned his Ph.D. at Vienna and studied in Berlin under Haupt, Bopp, Ranke, and Müllenhoff. He held professorships at Vienna (1868–1872), Strasbourg (1872), and Berlin (1877).

Wilhelm Schmidt worked in linguistics and religious studies, studying at Berlin and Vienna. He directed the Anima Mundi Museum (1927) and Anthropos Institute (1931), and held professorships at the University of Vienna (1925–1938) and the University of Fribourg (from 1939).

Wilhelm Schott specialized in Sinology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Giessen, Halle (Ph.D.), and Berlin. He held posts as Privatdozent at Halle and Berlin, where he served as apl. Professor from 1838 to 1884.

Wilhelm Schulze specialized in linguistics and Indology, studying at Berlin under Steinthal and Schmidt, and Greifswald under Zimmer. He held chairs at the University of Göttingen (1895) and Humboldt University of Berlin (1902–1932).

Wilhelm Siegling focused on Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied under Richard Pischel (Ph.D. Berlin, 1906) and Emil Sieg, later holding posts at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin (1907) and the Prussian Academy of Sciences (1912).

Wilhelm Solf was an Indology scholar who studied at Berlin, Kiel, Göttingen, and Halle (PhD under Richard Pischel, ~1885–1886), later completing a Dr.iuris at Jena (~1894–1896). He also held a post at Kiel University.

Wilhelm Storck specialized in linguistics and other fields. He studied at Munich, Münster, Bonn, and Berlin (Ph.D. under Franz Bopp and Albrecht Weber), and served as ao. Professor of German Language and Literature at the University of Münster from 1862.

Wilhelm Streitberg was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. He studied at Leipzig (Dr. phil. 1888) and Münster (habilitation 1889). He held professorships at Fribourg (1889–1898), Münster (1899–1909), and Munich (1909–1920), before teaching at Leipzig (1920–1925).

Wilhelm Tomaschek specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, history and archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Vienna (1860–1864) and held professorships in geography at the University of Graz (1877, 1881) and Vienna (1885).

Wilhelm Vatke was a scholar of religious studies and philosophy. He studied at the University of Halle-Wittenberg, Humboldt University of Berlin, and the University of Göttingen, and held a post at Humboldt University of Berlin from around 1830 to 1882.

Wilhelm Volck was a scholar of religious studies, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Erlangen-Nuremberg and Leipzig, later serving as professor of Semitic Philology at Tartu (1864–1898) and professor of Old Testament Exegesis at Rostock (1900).

Wilhelm Wackernagel was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (1824–1827) under Karl Lachmann and August Boeckh, and served as Ordinarius at the University of Basel from 1835 to 1869.

Wilhelm Wissmann was a linguist who earned his Ph.D. at Humboldt University of Berlin under Wilhelm Schulze. He held professorships at the University of Freiburg (1940), the University of Königsberg (1942), and the University of Munich (from 1953).

Wilhelm Wundt worked in philosophy and related fields. He studied at the University of Tübingen, Heidelberg University, and Humboldt University of Berlin, later holding posts at Zurich (1857), Leipzig (1858), and Heidelberg (1864).
